mainTopic: A dog or goat that jumps and does damage (normal versus unusual behavior), and the dispute between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about why a person is liable for damage done by his fire.
overview: The גמרא first raises a contradiction. A ברייתא says a jumping dog or goat is פטור, even though the teaching just before said the owner pays in full. רב פפא explains that the ברייתא is talking about unusual movement: a dog that leaped and a goat that climbed. Even then, פטור only means פטור from נזק שלם, and the owner still pays חצי נזק. Next the גמרא brings a basic dispute about fire. רבי יוחנן says אשו משום חציו (fire is like a person's arrows), and ריש לקיש says אשו משום ממונו (fire is like his property). Each one explains why he rejects the other's comparison. The גמרא then tests ריש לקיש against the משנה of the dog that carried a burning cake, and ריש לקיש answers that the dog threw the coal. It also tests him against the משנה of the camel loaded with flax. ריש לקיש explains that the camel lit every spot itself, and that in the storekeeper's case the camel had stopped to urinate.

steps.title: A teaching says a jumping dog or goat is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the earlier ruling with a ברייתא that says a dog or goat that jumped is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: if a dog or a goat jumped, whether from above to below or from below to above, the owners are exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to contradict what was just taught. The earlier teaching said the owner pays full damage, but this ברייתא says he is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier teaching treated jumping as normal behavior for a dog or goat, so the owner pays נזק שלם. This ברייתא says פטורין, which looks like a direct clash. The גמרא now has to explain how both teachings can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught in a ברייתא (introduces a contradicting source)

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: a dog or a goat that jumped;
whether from above to below,
or from below to above, they are exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling stated just before this section, that a jumping dog or goat makes the owner pay full damage.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier ruling that the owner pays נזק שלם when a dog or goat jumps and does damage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says the very same case is פטור, so the two teachings seem to contradict each other.

steps.title: רב פפא: the animals moved in an unusual way
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the ברייתא is talking about animals that moved in a way that is not normal for them: a dog that leaped and a goat that climbed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא explained it: their ways of moving were switched. The dog moved by leaping, and the goat moved by climbing.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא solves the contradiction by saying the ברייתא is describing a different, unusual kind of movement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ruling was about normal jumping, which is expected behavior, so the owner pays in full. The ברייתא is about each animal moving in a way that is not typical for it. Unusual behavior gets different rules, so the two teachings no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: Their way of moving was switched

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'switched' as the dog and goat swapping places. It means each one moved in a way that is not normal for its kind.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa interpreted it:
Their manner was changed:
the dog by leaping, and the goat by climbing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction by limiting the ברייתא to an unusual case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each teaching is about a different kind of movement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both teachings seemed to be about the same normal jumping.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about unusual movement (a leaping dog, a climbing goat), while the earlier ruling is about normal movement.

steps.title: Then why should they be fully exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even if the movement was unusual, the animal still did damage, so why are the owners exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why are they exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב פפא's answer. Unusual behavior should not lead to a complete exemption.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unusual damage by an animal still makes the owner liable in some way. So saying פטורין in the unusual case seems too strong. The גמרא needs to explain what פטורין really means here.

phrases.english: If so, why are they exempt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's explanation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word פטורין in the ברייתא, as רב פפא explained it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Unusual damage still brings some liability, so a full exemption does not make sense.

steps.title: Exempt from full damage, but they pay half
steps.stepSummary: The answer: פטורין means exempt from נזק שלם, but the owners still pay חצי נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are exempt from full damage, and they are liable for half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the ברייתא's 'exempt' is only partial. The owner still pays half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unusual behavior by an animal brings payment of חצי נזק, not נזק שלם. So the ברייתא only meant that the owner does not pay the full amount. This completes רב פפא's answer, and the contradiction is fully settled.
steps.whatToRemember: Normal jumping by a dog or goat means נזק שלם. Unusual movement (a leaping dog, a climbing goat) means חצי נזק. The ברייתא's פטורין only means exempt from full damage.

phrases.english: Exempt from full damage,
and they are liable for half damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: פָּטוּר מִנֶּזֶק שָׁלֵם, וְחַיָּיבִין בַּחֲצִי נֶזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by narrowing what 'exempt' means.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a word: פטורין means only partly exempt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: פטורין meant no payment at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Exempt only from נזק שלם; they pay חצי נזק.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: a dog that took a cake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the opening words of the next case in the משנה, a dog that took a burning cake, to begin discussing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה said:] A dog that took...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a heading. The גמרא names the next part of the משנה it is about to discuss, which sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case is a dog that took a cake with a coal attached and set a stack of grain on fire. Damage from fire raises the question of why a person pays for fire at all. That question is the dispute that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A dog that took (the opening words of the משנה's case)

phrases.english: A dog that took.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opens discussion of the משנה's case of the dog that took a cake and burned a stack of grain.

steps.title: Is fire like arrows or like property?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says a person's fire is like his arrows. ריש לקיש says a person's fire is like his property.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רבי יוחנן says: his fire is because of his arrows. And ריש לקיש says: his fire is because of his property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a basic argument about why a person pays when his fire spreads and does damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן compares fire to arrows: it is as if the person himself shot something at a distance. ריש לקיש compares fire to a person's belongings, like his animal, which he must guard so it does not cause damage. Both agree he pays; they argue about which kind of liability fire is.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a dispute between אמוראים)
His arrows (damage done by the person himself)

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree the owner pays for his fire. The argument is only about which kind of liability fire is: like the person's own action, or like damage done by his belongings.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic חקירה in דיני נזיקין. Whether fire counts as the person's own act or as his property's damage shapes how the laws of fire work in the rest of the סוגיא.

phrases.english: It was stated: Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
His fire is because of his arrows.
phrases.notes: He means fire is treated like an arrow the person shot himself.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says:
His fire is because of his property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a basic dispute about fire, which the משנה's case involves.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: fire is like arrows (the person's own act). ריש לקיש: fire is like property (damage by one's belongings).

steps.title: Why doesn't ריש לקיש agree with רבי יוחנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what bothered ריש לקיש about comparing fire to arrows.
steps.simpleTranslation: And ריש לקיש, what is the reason he did not say like רבי יוחנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why ריש לקיש rejected the arrow comparison. It is setting up his explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Comparing fire to arrows seems reasonable, since in both cases the person starts something that does damage far away. So the גמרא wants to know what ריש לקיש saw as different.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish, what is the reason
he did not say like Rabbi Yoḥanan?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָמַר כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind ריש לקיש's view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why ריש לקיש does not accept the comparison of fire to arrows.

steps.title: Arrows travel by his force; fire does not
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש's reason: an arrow moves by the person's own force, but fire moves on its own (with the wind).
steps.simpleTranslation: He would tell you: his arrows go by his force, but this fire does not go by his force.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives ריש לקיש's reason for rejecting the arrow comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An arrow flies only because the person shot it, so the damage is his own direct act. Fire spreads without the person pushing it, so it is not his own force. That is why ריש לקיש treats fire like property the owner must guard.

keyTerms.meaning: By his force, by his own power

phrases.english: He would say to you: his arrows go by his force,
this one does not go by his force.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about ריש לקיש's reasoning.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Arrows move by the person's force; fire does not, so fire cannot be compared to arrows.

steps.title: Why doesn't רבי יוחנן agree with ריש לקיש?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what bothered רבי יוחנן about comparing fire to property.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן, what is the reason he did not say like ריש לקיש?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks the same question from the other side. It is setting up רבי יוחנן's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Treating fire like an animal that wanders off and does damage also seems reasonable. The גמרא wants to know what רבי יוחנן saw as different.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan, what is the reason
he did not say like Reish Lakish?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָמַר כְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same question as step 7, now asked about רבי יוחנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יוחנן does not accept the comparison of fire to property.

steps.title: Property is tangible; fire is not
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's reason: property is a real, solid thing, but fire has no real substance.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would tell you: property has substance, but this fire has no substance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי יוחנן's reason for rejecting the property comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability for property is about a real object that a person owns, like an animal. Fire is not a solid thing that can be owned in that way, so it cannot be treated as his property. That is why רבי יוחנן treats fire as the person's own act, like arrows.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן: fire is like arrows, because fire has no substance and cannot be property. ריש לקיש: fire is like property, because fire does not move by the person's own force the way an arrow does.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָךְ: מָמוֹנָא – אִית בֵּיהּ מַמָּשָׁא,
phrases.english: He would say to you: property has substance,
this does not have substance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ: מָמוֹנָא אִית בֵּיהּ מַמָּשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about רבי יוחנן's reasoning.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Property is a tangible thing; fire is not, so fire cannot be compared to property.

steps.title: Bringing the משנה of the dog and the burning cake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a dog that took a cake and burned a grain stack. It shows that this fits easily with the view that fire is like arrows.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: 'A dog that took a cake...' This works well for the one who says fire is like arrows, because the fire is the dog's 'arrows.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to test the מחלוקת. First it shows the side that has no problem, and this sets up a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the owner of the dog pays half damage for the grain stack. According to רבי יוחנן, the fire the dog carried is like an arrow the dog 'shot,' so the dog's owner is responsible for it. The word בשלמא ('granted') tells us a 'but' is coming against the other opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: A cake baked right on hot coals
Granted, this works well for one side (a challenge to the other side is coming)
His arrows: damage done by his own force

phrases.english: We learned: A dog that took a cake, etc.
phrases.notes: The משנה goes on: the dog took the cake with a coal stuck to it, ate it near a grain stack, and the stack caught fire.

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says:
his fire is because of his arrows,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יוחנן's opinion from step 6.

phrases.english: it is the arrows of the dog.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both reasons were explained, the גמרא now tests the מחלוקת against a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: Whether fire is like arrows (רבי יוחנן) or like property (ריש לקיש)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the dog that took a burning cake and burned a grain stack

steps.title: The challenge to ריש לקיש: the fire was not the dog owner's property
steps.stepSummary: If fire is like property, why does the dog's owner pay at all? The fire belonged to the cake's owner, not to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for the one who says fire is like property: this fire is not the property of the dog's owner!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש using the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש makes a person responsible for fire because it is his property, like his animal. Here the coal belonged to the owner of the cake, so it was never the dog owner's property. So why does the משנה make the dog's owner pay for the stack?

phrases.english: But according to the one who says:
his fire is because of his property,
this fire is not the property
of the dog's owner!
phrases.notes: The coal came with the cake, so it belonged to the cake's owner, not the dog owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר: אִשּׁוֹ מִשּׁוּם מָמוֹנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the בשלמא/אלא pattern by attacking the second opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that fire is like property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה makes the dog's owner pay for the stack, but under 'property' logic he should not pay, because the fire was not his.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: the dog threw the coal, so the owner pays only for the spot it hit
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that the dog threw the coal onto the stack. The owner pays full for the cake, half for the spot the coal hit, and nothing for the rest of the stack.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש can say: Here the dog threw the coal. For the cake he pays full damage, for the spot of the coal he pays half damage, and for the rest of the stack he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the challenge by explaining the case in the משנה differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The half payment in the משנה is not for the fire spreading. It is only for the exact spot where the thrown coal landed, like the half payment for צרורות (things an animal kicks or flings). The spreading fire was not the dog owner's property, so for the rest of the stack he is פטור, just as ריש לקיש's view requires.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (a way of narrowing the case)
The spot where the coal landed
Half the cost of the damage

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think ריש לקיש's half damage is for the fire. It is only for the small spot the thrown coal hit. For the fire spreading through the stack, he pays nothing.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish can say to you:
Here, what are we dealing with?
Where it threw it.
phrases.notes: The dog flung the coal onto the stack instead of putting it down.

phrases.english: For the cake he pays full damage,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל מָקוֹם גַּחֶלֶת מְשַׁלֵּם חֲצִי נֶזֶק,
phrases.english: and for the spot of the coal he pays half damage,
and for the whole stack he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (the dog threw the coal)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The half damage in the משנה is for the fire burning the stack, which would not fit ריש לקיש.
steps.terutzMaskana: The half damage is only for the spot the thrown coal hit (צרורות). For the spreading fire the owner is exempt, which fits ריש לקיש.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the dog placed the coal down, so the owner pays half for the stack
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads the משנה simply: the dog put the cake and coal down on the stack. The owner pays full for the cake and the coal's spot, and half for the rest of the stack.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן says the dog placed it down. For the cake and the spot of the coal he pays full damage, and for the stack he pays half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how רבי יוחנן reads the same משנה, to contrast it with ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the dog placed the coal directly, damage to the cake and the coal's spot is direct damage, so the owner pays full. The fire spreading through the rest of the stack is the dog's 'arrows,' an indirect result of its force like צרורות, so he pays half. Here the half payment really is for the fire, unlike ריש לקיש's reading.

keyTerms.meaning: The full cost of the damage

steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions fit the משנה, but they read it differently. ריש לקיש: the dog threw the coal, so half for the spot and nothing for the stack. רבי יוחנן: the dog placed the coal, so full for the spot and half for the stack.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan:
Where it placed it down.
For the cake and for the spot of the coal
he pays full damage,
and for the stack he pays half damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts רבי יוחנן's reading of the משנה with ריש לקיש's reading in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the case in its simple way (the dog placed the coal)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without ריש לקיש's 'threw' reading, the משנה looks like the dog just put the coal down.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי יוחנן the simple reading works: full for direct damage, half for the spreading fire as the dog's arrows.

steps.title: The camel loaded with flax
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: a camel loaded with flax catches fire from a storekeeper's lamp and burns a building. The camel's owner pays. If the lamp was placed outside, the storekeeper pays. רבי יהודה exempts the storekeeper if it was a נר חנוכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A camel loaded with flax was walking in the public street. Its flax went into a store and caught fire from the storekeeper's lamp, and the fire burned the building. The camel's owner must pay. If the storekeeper put his lamp outside, the storekeeper must pay. רבי יהודה says: if it was a נר חנוכה, he does not have to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new משנה to test the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. This step only sets out the case; the challenge comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two people's things are involved: the camel's flax and the storekeeper's lamp. The fire itself started from the storekeeper's lamp, yet the camel's owner pays. That is the detail the גמרא will focus on next.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source
flax, a plant fiber that burns very easily
the lamp lit for חנוכה, which is a מצוה to place outside

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A camel loaded with flax
was passing through the public domain;
its flax went into the store
and it caught fire from the storekeeper's lamp,
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'they caught fire' (round brackets); the corrected wording in square brackets says 'it,' meaning the flax, caught fire.

phrases.english: and it set the building on fire —
the camel's owner is liable.
If the storekeeper placed his lamp outside —
the storekeeper is liable.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
With a Chanukah lamp, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing with the dog משנה, the גמרא brings a second משנה to test the same argument.
steps.raayaObject: Whether fire is like arrows (רבי יוחנן) or like property (ריש לקיש).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about a camel loaded with flax (later in בבא קמא).

steps.title: Why does the camel's owner pay if the fire isn't his?
steps.stepSummary: This fits easily with אשו משום חציו, since the burning flax is the camel's 'arrow.' But according to אשו משום ממונו, the fire is not the camel owner's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for the one who says a person's fire is like his arrows: this is the camel's arrow. But for the one who says fire is like his property: this fire is not the property of the camel's owner!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש: in this case the camel's owner pays for a fire that was never his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If fire is like arrows, whoever pushes the fire forward is responsible, and the camel pushed it. If fire is like property, you only pay for fire that belongs to you, and this fire came from the storekeeper's lamp. This is the same kind of attack the גמרא made with the dog in step 12.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (for one view, but not the other)
his fire is like his arrows
his fire is like his property

phrases.english: It makes sense according to the one who says
his fire is because of his arrows —
these are the camel's arrows.
But according to the one who says it is because of his property —

phrases.aramaic: הַאי אֵשׁ, לָאו מָמוֹנָא דְּבַעַל גָּמָל הוּא!
phrases.english: this fire is not the property of the camel's owner!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אִשּׁוֹ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ruling of the משנה in step 15 against ריש לקיש.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that fire is like property.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The camel's owner pays, yet the fire was not his property, so the 'property' view seems unable to explain why he pays.

steps.title: The camel set the whole building on fire itself
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers that the camel moved around and lit every part of the building directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש could say to you: What case are we dealing with here? The camel went around and set fire to the whole building, every part of it.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש explains that the camel itself spread the burning flax to every spot in the building.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the camel touched each part of the building with the burning flax, the fire never had to spread on its own. The camel did the damage directly, much like an animal causing damage with its body. So the camel's owner pays even though the fire was not his. This is like his answer about the dog in step 13.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (the גמרא narrows the case)
moving around and lighting spot after spot

phrases.english: Reish Lakish could say to you:
With what are we dealing here?
Where it went around setting fire to the entire building, all of it.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the camel. It carried the burning flax from spot to spot, so the fire never had to spread by itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fire spread through the building on its own, so the camel's owner is paying for someone else's fire.
steps.terutzMaskana: The camel lit each spot directly, so its owner pays for what the camel did, not for owning the fire.

steps.title: Then why does the storekeeper pay in the next part?
steps.stepSummary: The next part of the משנה says the storekeeper pays if his lamp was outside. If the camel lit every spot itself, why should the storekeeper pay?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the next part of the משנה: if the storekeeper put his lamp outside, the storekeeper pays. If the camel went around lighting everything, why should he pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks ריש לקיש's answer by looking at the next part of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the camel spread the fire to every spot, then the camel did all the damage. The storekeeper's lamp only started the flax burning. So why would the storekeeper be blamed for the whole building?

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your answer is right)
the later part of the משנה

phrases.english: If so, say the latter clause:
If the storekeeper placed his lamp outside —
the storekeeper is liable.
But if it went around setting fires — why is he liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges ריש לקיש's answer in step 17 from the later part of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the camel lit every spot (מְסַכְסֶכֶת).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the camel did all the burning, the storekeeper should not be liable, yet the משנה says he is.

steps.title: The camel stood still
steps.stepSummary: The answer: in the second case the camel stood still, and the burning flax caught the building all at once.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where the camel stood still.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that in the storekeeper's case the camel did not walk around but stood in one place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the camel did not move around, it did not carry the fire from spot to spot. The huge load of burning flax caught the building all at once. So the blame falls on the storekeeper, who put his lamp in the street.

phrases.english: Where it stood still.
phrases.notes: This is only about the later part of the משנה, where the lamp was outside. The first part is still the case where the camel moved around.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 by saying the later part of the משנה is a different case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the first part is a moving camel, the later part a standing camel.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both parts of the משנה describe a camel moving around.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the later part the camel stood still, so the camel did not spread the fire and the storekeeper is to blame.

steps.title: A camel standing still should make its owner even more liable
steps.stepSummary: If the camel stood still and set the building on fire, the camel's owner should be all the more liable and the storekeeper exempt, since the owner should have moved it away.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the camel stood still and lit the building, then all the more so the storekeeper should be exempt and the camel's owner liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer: a camel standing still makes its owner look even more at fault.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A camel walking past might be an accident. But if it stood still next to a lamp, its owner had time to move it away and didn't. So standing still should make the camel's owner pay, not the storekeeper.

keyTerms.meaning: exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: If it stood still and set fire —
all the more so the storekeeper should be exempt
and the camel's owner liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: עָמְדָה וְסִכְסְכָה – כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן דְּחֶנְווֹנִי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the camel stood still.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Standing still means the camel's owner was careless for not moving it, so he should pay and the storekeeper should not.

steps.title: The camel stopped to urinate
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח, quoting רב איקא, says the camel stopped to urinate, so its owner could not move it. That is why the storekeeper pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר מנוח said in the name of רב איקא: What case are we dealing with here? The camel stopped in order to urinate.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בר מנוח explains why the camel stood still: it stopped to urinate, so its owner had no way to move it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A camel that stops to urinate cannot be made to move, so its owner is not careless for letting it stand there. The fault goes back to the storekeeper, who put his lamp in the street. With this, the משנה fits ריש לקיש in both of its parts.
steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש explains the camel משנה with two different cases. In the first part, the camel's owner pays because the camel moved around and lit everything itself. In the later part, the storekeeper pays because the camel had to stand still to urinate, so its owner was not at fault.

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Manoah said
in the name of Rav Ika:
With what are we dealing here?
For example, where it stood still to urinate;
phrases.notes: A camel can't be moved while it does this, so the owner had no chance to pull it away from the lamp.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by giving a reason the camel stood still that is not the owner's fault.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the camel was standing still for a reason its owner could not control.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A camel standing still means its owner was careless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The camel stopped to urinate and could not be moved, so its owner is not at fault and the storekeeper pays.
